tip: Words on screen that show what is said and described, for people who cannot hear it.
meaning: Captions write down the speech and also important sounds, like [laughter]. They help people who are deaf, and everybody who watches without sound.
example: On a train, you watch a video with the sound off, and captions let you follow the story.
vukem: A caption is word-timed text on a caption track. See [Text and captions](/docs/guide/text-and-captions).

tip: Words on screen that translate or write down what is said.
meaning: Subtitles usually write what people say, often in another language. They assume the viewer can hear the sound.
example: A cartoon in Japanese with English words at the bottom.

tip: Captions drawn into the picture so they cannot be turned off.
meaning: Open (burned-in) captions are part of the video image. Every viewer sees them, on every app. They cannot be switched off or changed.
example: Short videos for social networks often have big words burned in.
vukem: Captions in Vukem Video are burned in when you export.

tip: Captions kept separate from the picture, so the viewer can turn them on or off.
meaning: Closed captions are a separate track of text. The player draws them, and the viewer chooses to show them (the CC button).
example: You press CC on a streaming service to read the words.

tip: The whole text of what is said in a video.
meaning: A transcript is a written copy of the speech. It can be with or without times.
example: The written version of a recorded interview.

tip: Turning speech into written words, by a person or by a program.
meaning: A transcription program listens to the audio and writes the words with the time when each one is spoken.
example: Your voice message turned into text.

tip: The exact start and end of every word, so words appear in time with the voice.
meaning: With word timing each word knows when it is said. This lets the caption highlight the word being spoken, like a karaoke screen.
example: In a short video the current word turns yellow as the person says it.
vukem: Every caption word has its own start and length.

tip: Words at the start of a video, or in it, that say what it is about.
meaning: A title card or title text names the video, a chapter or a place. It is different from captions, which write the speech.
example: "Summer 2026" appears at the start of a holiday video.

tip: A small name tag in the bottom part of the screen.
meaning: A lower third is text in the lower third of the picture, like a person's name when they first speak.
example: A news report shows "Ana Silva, Scientist" under a person.

tip: The list of people who worked on a video, shown at the end.
meaning: Credits thank the people and name the roles. In movies they roll up the screen at the end.
example: The names scroll upwards after the film is over.

tip: A set of letters, numbers and signs with one style of drawing.
meaning: A font decides how letters look. Some are plain, some playful, some formal.
example: A birthday card in a curly font looks friendlier than one in a strict font.
vukem: Import your own with `font_import`, then add it with `font.add`. See [Brand kit](/docs/guide/brand-kit).

tip: Serif letters have little feet; sans-serif letters are plain.
meaning: A serif font has small strokes at the ends of letters, like in a book. Sans-serif ("without feet") is cleaner and is common on screens.
example: Books use serif letters; most phone apps use sans-serif.

tip: How thin or thick the letters are, like light, regular or bold.
meaning: Weight makes letters thicker or thinner. Bold stands out, light is calm.
example: A title in bold and a note in light.

tip: Adjusting the space between two particular letters.
meaning: Some pairs of letters, like A and V, look too far apart. Kerning moves them closer so the word looks even.
example: The gap between A and V in "AVA" is made smaller.

tip: The space between all the letters of a text.
meaning: Wider spacing looks airy and calm. Tighter spacing looks dense and strong.
example: Small capital words look good with wider spacing.

tip: The space between lines of text.
meaning: Leading (pronounced "ledding") is how far apart two lines are. Too tight and lines touch; too loose and they look like separate sentences.
example: A caption in two lines that are easy to read.

tip: The place where a text goes on to the next line.
meaning: Good captions break lines at natural places, like after a comma, so each line is easy to read in one glance.
example: "I love my new" / "red bicycle" is better than "I love" / "my new red bicycle".

tip: An outline around letters, so they can be read on any background.
meaning: A stroke is a thin border around the letters. A white text with a dark outline is readable on both dark and light pictures.
example: White letters with a black outline over a bright sky.

tip: A soft shadow behind text or a shape, so it seems to float.
meaning: A shadow makes text stand out from the picture. A light, small shadow looks best.
example: A title that seems to float above the video.

tip: Whether text lines up on the left, in the middle or on the right.
meaning: Centre alignment is common for captions and titles. Left alignment is common for paragraphs.
example: Captions are usually centred under the picture.

tip: The part of the screen where text will not be cut off or covered.
meaning: Apps put buttons and names over the video, and some screens cut the edges. Keeping text inside the safe area makes sure people can read it.
example: On a short video the bottom is covered by the caption and the heart button, so the words go higher.
vukem: The lint checks text against the safe area. See [Safe area](/docs/guide/safe-area).

tip: How fast a viewer can read the captions, in characters or words per second.
meaning: Captions need to stay on screen long enough to be read. About 15 to 20 characters per second is a common limit for adults.
example: A sentence that flashes by in half a second is too fast.

tip: A very common caption file: a list of numbered texts with start and end times.
meaning: An SRT file is plain text. Each block has a number, a time range and the words. Almost every player can read it.

tip: The caption file format used by web browsers.
meaning: WebVTT is like SRT with extras for position and style. It works with the video tag in web pages.
example: A website that shows captions under its own video player.

tip: A caption file format used by broadcasters and streaming services.
meaning: TTML is an XML format for timed text, with detailed positions and colours. Streaming and TV use it.
example: Captions delivered to a TV channel.

tip: Replacing the voices with another language's voices.
meaning: Dubbing records new voices in another language and puts them in place of the original ones. Subtitles instead keep the original voices.
example: A cartoon spoken in French, dubbed into Portuguese.

tip: Making words move in, out or around.
meaning: Text animation can fade, pop, slide or typewriter the words. It catches attention but it should not make text hard to read.
example: A title that pops in with a bounce.
vukem: `text.apply_preset` has six presets. See [Effects and color](/docs/guide/effects-and-color).

tip: A name before a line, to show who is speaking.
meaning: When people talk off screen, or two voices overlap, a label like "ANA:" tells the viewer who speaks.
example: "MOM: Dinner is ready!" in the captions.

tip: The system that gives a number to every letter, sign and emoji of every language.
meaning: Thanks to Unicode a video editor can write Chinese, Portuguese accents and emoji in the same title.
example: The letter "ã" and the emoji "😀" both have a Unicode number.
